case_study_insert.main_stem: Carrowdale Hall (CDH) is a private limited company in the hospitality and events sector, employing a workforce of 64. Founded in 2009 by Elena Carrow, the business operates a heritage wedding and conference venue on the shores of Lake Carrow and uses a hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership. CDH plans to invest $1,450,000 in a new lakeside events pavilion with 400 covers, financed by an $800,000 ten-year bank loan and $650,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $216,000 a year, a variable cost of $46 a unit and a selling price of $70, and currently produces 15,000 units a year. CDH faces two operational problems: labour turnover in the banqueting team has reached 17% and food waste from events is rising.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Market Research Summary — August 2026: A survey of 480 couples and corporate clients found 73% prefer all-inclusive event packages, 61% would pay up to $12 extra per guest for locally sourced catering, and 48% say on-site accommodation influenced their venue choice. Carrowdale Hall staged 132 events last year at an average spend of $14,500 per wedding and $6,200 per conference. Complaints fell from 29 to 17 per quarter, and the lead time from enquiry to signed contract is 5.5 weeks. A skills audit found 22 of 64 banqueting staff have not completed on-the-job training on the pavilion catering equipment; off-the-job courses at the regional college cost $850 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Carrowdale Hall as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, its third rise this year, increasing costs for businesses servicing variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.9% from $11.85 to $12.55 per hour from April 2026, lifting hospitality staffing costs. (3) Wholesale catering input costs have risen 9.6% year-on-year and food inflation stands at 7.0%, while consumer spending on weddings and conferences grew 4.8% over the same period.

questions.question_text: CDH plans to finance part of the lakeside pavilion with an $800,000 ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for CDH of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of a larger bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using retained profit costs CDH nothing in interest or repayment charges, which protects its cash flow at a time when the $800,000 bank loan would already commit fixed repayments on top of fixed costs of $216,000 a year. With the base rate now at 5.25%, interest on an even larger loan would absorb more of the $24 contribution earned on every $70 cover, so retained profit keeps more of the 15,000 units' revenue available to fund the pavilion build and to absorb the 9.6% rise in catering input costs.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and condition risk attached to a bigger bank loan. If wedding and conference demand softens (the wider market grew only 4.8% last year), CDH would not face repossession of the lakeside pavilion or Lake Carrow assets, and Elena Carrow retains full ownership and control without lender conditions on how the pavilion and its 400 covers are run. The $650,000 retained profit is also available immediately without application delays, letting CDH lock in the 132-events pipeline and the 5.5-week contract lead time while rivals wait for credit approval.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development applied to Carrowdale Hall's expansion, costs and market.

questions.question_text: CDH is launching its new lakeside events pavilion. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should CDH choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television campaign: TV would give the pavilion launch mass reach and instant brand awareness among couples and corporate event planners nationwide. However, production and airtime costs are extremely high, much of the audience neither marries in nor books conferences in the Lake Carrow region, so wasted spend would be severe for a 64-employee business already funding an $1,450,000 build. TV also cannot show the all-inclusive, locally sourced story to a targeted segment with any measurable booking response.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio is far cheaper, reaches the regional wedding and conference catchment, and suits time-sensitive launch messages. Its reach, however, stops at the region, while CDH's conference ambitions draw from much wider catchments; frequency would be low, listeners are not necessarily active venue buyers, and impact is hard to measure against the 5.5-week enquiry-to-contract cycle.

Social media influencer marketing: Food, wedding and corporate-events influencers would reach exactly the 73% preferring all-inclusive packages, the 61% willing to pay $12 extra per guest for locally sourced catering and the 48% influenced by on-site accommodation — audiences already primed by short-form venue tours. Cost per reached buyer is low, bookings are measurable from enquiry to signed contract, and the content doubles as proof of the pavilion experience during launch season.

Recommendation: CDH should choose social media influencer marketing. It targets the precise segments identified in CDH's own research at a fraction of TV's cost, scales beyond the local radio footprint, and showcases the all-inclusive, locally sourced offer. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a 64-person venue financing the build with an $800,000 bank loan; local radio is rejected as too narrow to fill a 400-cover pavilion. CDH should still add modest local print and an open-day press push to convert nearby demand as the bookings diary fills.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of CDH with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of CDH with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: CDH's labour turnover in the banqueting team has reached 17%. Explain two benefits for CDH of introducing democratic leadership to improve motivation in its banqueting team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives banqueting staff a genuine voice in shift patterns, event set-ups and portion routines on the pavilion, satisfying social and esteem needs (Maslow) and raising job satisfaction. Staff who help shape how 132 events a year are run are more likely to attend consistently and stay, directly attacking CDH's 17% labour turnover and reducing the recruitment and retraining burden on a workforce of 64.

Point 2: Involving staff surfaces practical fixes from the people handling food and guests daily, which cuts the complaints trend (29 to 17 per quarter) further and tackles the rising food waste. Motivated, listened-to staff also embrace the pavilion's catering equipment far more willingly, protecting service quality during the 5.5-week booking surge, and the commitment created reduces the risk that the April 2026 rise to $12.55 per hour becomes a flashpoint — democratic consultation values staff beyond pay alone, which a pure pay settlement cannot buy.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to CDH's turnover, complaints and pavilion opening.

questions.question_text: CDH must train 22 banqueting staff on the pavilion catering equipment. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the regional college. Which should CDH choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training on the pavilion's own catering equipment during live service is directly relevant, costs nothing in fees, keeps all 22 staff productive through the 132-event season and avoids disrupting the 5.5-week contract cycle. Head waiters coach machine-specific routines in real conditions; drawbacks are that mistakes can hit a 400-cover event in progress, bad habits may be passed on, and formal certification for auditors and insurers is limited.

Off-the-job training: The regional college course at $850 per employee gives structured, up-to-date catering and hygiene standards with recognised certification — $18,700 for all 22 staff, affordable against an $1,450,000 investment and $650,000 retained profit. However, it removes staff from the floor for days at a time, colliding with peak banqueting weeks, and the generic curriculum may not match CDH's pavilion menu, portion sizes and equipment settings, so on-site follow-up would still be needed.

Decision: CDH should choose on-the-job training as its primary route, supplemented by one off-the-job course day per shift leader at the regional college and a follow-up assessment in week four of the opening. This keeps capacity intact while turnover is already 17%, costs far less than $18,700 across the whole team, and delivers machine-specific competence immediately ahead of the opening season. Full off-the-job training is rejected because it would sideline a third of the banqueting workforce before the pavilion opens, risking delivery failures on contracted weddings and conferences; CDH can add certified college courses later for permanent senior hires and for new recruits as the pavilion beds in.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to CDH.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of CDH.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of CDH with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and pavilion relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how CDH's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $216,000 ÷ ($70 − $46) = $216,000 ÷ $24 = 9,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 9,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $70 − $46 = $24.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $24.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways CDH's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. CDH's management can compare the 9,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 15,000 units to confirm the pavilion is comfortably profitable, with a margin of safety of 6,000 units, informing whether to ramp up bookings beyond 132 events a year.
2. Contribution per unit of $24 lets CDH model price rises to offset the 9.6% catering input-cost inflation — for example, adding $5 per cover lifts contribution to $29 — and test whether all-inclusive packages still cover fixed costs of $216,000.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $216,000 and contribution per unit helps management check the new pavilion can also service the $800,000 ten-year bank loan on top of existing overheads before phase-two spending is approved.
4. Managers can use unit cost data ($216,000 ÷ 15,000 units + $46 = $60.40 a unit) to benchmark catering efficiency across events, attack the rising food waste from weddings and set menu pricing that protects the $14,500 average wedding spend.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 9,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $24 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety (6,000 units vs 15,000 output) confirms pavilion launch headroom; contribution modelling absorbs the 9.6% input-inflation squeeze on the $46 unit cost; fixed-cost coverage tests the $800,000 bank loan alongside $216,000 fixed costs; and unit cost of $60.40 benchmarks catering efficiency and food-waste control across the 132-event programme.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate CDH's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has CDH's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.50 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.54 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.02 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.23 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $150,000 inventories + $260,000 trade receivables + $55,000 cash = $465,000; 2025 current assets = $110,000 + $340,000 + $90,000 = $540,000. 2024 = $465,000 ÷ $310,000 = 1.50 : 1; 2025 = $540,000 ÷ $350,000 = 1.54 : 1. Excluding inventories: 2024 = ($465,000 − $150,000) ÷ $310,000 = $315,000 ÷ $310,000 = 1.02 : 1; 2025 = ($540,000 − $110,000) ÷ $350,000 = $430,000 ÷ $350,000 = 1.23 : 1.

Evaluation: Liquidity has clearly strengthened. Cover from current assets rose from 1.50 to 1.54, while current liabilities grew only from $310,000 to $350,000 against a $75,000 increase in current assets — the pavilion preparation year was already partly pre-financed, and inventories fell to $110,000 as catering purchasing tightened. The inventory-excluded measure improved from 1.02 to 1.23, so CDH no longer leans on selling perishable stock to meet short-term debts — a critical buffer while it services an $800,000 ten-year bank loan. However, trade receivables rose from $260,000 to $340,000 (+31%), outstripping asset growth; conference and wedding clients on extended credit could slow cash inflows mid-build. Cash rose from $55,000 to $90,000, cushioning but not eliminating that risk.

Conclusion: CDH's financial position has improved. Liquidity is stronger on both measures and the improvement does not depend on inventory. The priority is tightening credit control with corporate clients and staging the pavilion drawdowns so receivables do not outrun the build, preserving CDH's capacity to fund the opening season.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether CDH's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for CDH of launching the pavilion with locally sourced catering packages.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Locally sourced catering matches the 61% of surveyed clients willing to pay up to $12 extra per guest and strengthens the all-inclusive story 73% prefer, protecting CDH's $24 contribution per unit even as catering input costs rise 9.6%. It also builds credibility with corporate conference organisers who need provenance stories for their own stakeholders, supporting premium pricing toward the $14,500 average wedding spend and helping fill the 400-cover pavilion in its first season.

Disadvantage: Locally sourced ingredients cost more and fluctuate with seasonal supply, pushing the $46 variable cost per unit upward and squeezing contribution unless the $12 premium is actually collected on every cover. Any supply inconsistency — a shortfall of lake fish or dairy from local farms the week of a 400-cover wedding — would risk the defect and waste problems CDH is already fighting, and could undo the complaint recovery (29 to 17 per quarter) just as the pavilion opens.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to CDH's research data, costs and pavilion expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 5.9% minimum wage increase and the 9.6% rise in catering input costs will affect CDH. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): If CDH's $800,000 ten-year bank loan, or any portion refinanced at today's rates, carries a variable rate, the 0.75 percentage point rise adds roughly $6,000 a year — meaningful against $216,000 fixed costs but absorbable. Higher rates also cool household discretionary spending on weddings, although CDH's corporate conference pipeline (conferences average $6,200 per event) is less rate-sensitive.

Minimum wage increase (5.9%, to $12.55): Hospitality is labour-intensive, and banqueting, kitchen and housekeeping roles concentrate near the minimum. If, for illustration, 40 of the 64 staff are near the minimum, the extra $0.70 per hour costs about $56,000 a year — a recurring hit equal to roughly a quarter of fixed costs, landing exactly when the pavilion opens and new staff are hired.

Catering input-cost inflation (9.6%): Food is the dominant element of the $46 unit cost. If, for illustration, ingredients are around half the unit cost (about $23), a 9.6% rise adds about $2.20 per cover; across 15,000 units that is roughly $33,000 a year, dragging contribution from $24 toward $21.80 at the worst moment, and it recurs on every cover rather than once a year.

Conclusion: The 9.6% rise in catering input costs will have the greatest impact. Unlike the wage rise, it cannot be avoided by hiring decisions or rota design; unlike the interest rise (about $6,000 a year, hedgeable by fixing the loan), it compounds on every one of the 15,000 units sold and cannot be fully recovered — clients sign all-inclusive budgets 5.5 weeks in advance, leaving CDH stuck with pre-agreed prices. The wage rise is the second most serious pressure; the interest rise is smallest and manageable. CDH should lock input-price contracts with lake-district suppliers, re-price packages from 2027, and fix its loan rate before April 2026.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to CDH.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on CDH's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of CDH with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
